entries.title: PlayStation 3
entries.subtitle: The console becomes a connected place
entries.summary: Blu-ray discs, a hard drive and PlayStation Network brought games, films and an expanding online world into one machine.
body: PlayStation 3 reached Japan on 11 November 2006 and North America six days later. Europe followed on 23 March 2007. There was no single worldwide launch day: players entered this generation at different times, and the software available around the machine changed as the rollout continued.

Sony's ambition extended beyond a faster games console. A Blu-ray drive offered another way to watch high-definition films, while a hard drive and PlayStation Network supported downloadable games and online services. The XrossMediaBar organised this growing collection of activities into rows of icons. The machine could be a disc player, a meeting point and a game library, sometimes in the same evening.

That wider role did not give the generation just one creative direction. Resistance explored a large-scale shooter, Uncharted built an adventure around characters and spectacle, and LittleBigPlanet invited players to make and share levels. The large, curved original console displayed here belongs to the beginning of that story. Smaller redesigns arrived in 2009 and 2012.

entries.title: PlayStation 4
entries.subtitle: A moment worth sharing
entries.summary: A new button on the controller made recording and sharing part of the console's everyday vocabulary.
body: The DualShock 4 carried a small but revealing change: a Share button. PlayStation 4 made capturing a surprising moment and showing it to someone else part of the console itself. Live streaming and, later, Share Play extended that idea. Playing a game and being an audience for a game were becoming closely connected experiences.

This was also the first PlayStation home console to reach North America before Japan. It launched there on 15 November 2013, followed by Europe on 29 November. The Japanese release came on 22 February 2014. Those regional dates are part of its history, rather than interchangeable labels for one global event.

The original machine's sloping black case gave this increasingly social platform a compact physical form. Its library could still offer solitary journeys: Bloodborne, Horizon Zero Dawn and God of War sat alongside experiences built around sharing a world with others. The console's cultural footprint includes both the games people played and the clips, broadcasts and conversations that travelled beyond them.

entries.title: PlayStation 5

date.region: Initial markets including Japan and North America

release_dates.region: United States, Canada, Mexico, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea
Europe and further announced rollout markets; mainland China followed separately

entries.subtitle: Changing the pace and feel of play
entries.summary: Fast storage and a new controller shifted attention towards the time spent waiting and the sensations carried through the hands.
body: A new console generation can change more than the picture. For PlayStation 5, Sony emphasised fast solid-state storage, 3D audio and the DualSense controller alongside its graphics hardware. The promise concerned the rhythm and feel of play: shorter loading waits, more detailed feedback and a stronger sense of being inside a space.

Two launch versions made the changing place of physical media visible. One included an Ultra HD Blu-ray drive; the Digital Edition omitted it. Both used the same core processor and storage technology. The choice concerned how a library would be acquired and kept, rather than a separate class of game.

The launch was staged. Seven markets, including Japan and the United States, received PS5 on 12 November 2020. Europe and further regions followed on 19 November. The tall white-and-black original body and DualSense became the recognisable objects of this transition. Here they sit at a still-open end of the museum's timeline: hardware whose history is continuing to be made.

entries.title: PlayStation Portable
entries.subtitle: The screen leaves the living room
entries.summary: Sony's first PlayStation handheld combined widescreen games, small optical discs and portable media playback.
body: PlayStation Portable asked what a PlayStation experience could become when its screen travelled with the player. The original PSP-1000 launched in Japan on 12 December 2004. North America followed on 24 March 2005 and Europe on 1 September. It was a new branch of the platform, rather than a home console made smaller.

Its UMD format put games and films on small enclosed optical discs. Wireless networking offered local and online connections, while music and video playback gave the hardware uses beyond a single game. The broad screen, speakers and controls presented a compact entertainment device at a time when those jobs had not yet converged around the modern smartphone.

The machine's identity also came from games that suited its particular setting. LocoRoco and Patapon found different ways to organise movement, rhythm and attention on a portable screen. The PSP could carry familiar PlayStation worlds, but it also made room for experiences shaped around a different object in the player's hands.

entries.title: PlayStation Vita

release_dates.region: North American and European general launch; some advance bundles earlier

entries.subtitle: A handheld with more ways in
entries.summary: Two analogue sticks, an OLED screen and touch surfaces on both sides invited different answers to what a portable game could be.
body: PlayStation Vita arrived in Japan on 17 December 2011. Its North American and European general release followed on 22 February 2012. Sony offered both Wi-Fi and 3G/Wi-Fi versions, treating portable play as something that could remain connected beyond the home.

The original machine put two analogue sticks beside a five-inch OLED touchscreen. Behind it was another touch surface; cameras and motion sensors added further possibilities. These were not simply extra specifications. They gave developers several ways to involve the player's hands, position and surroundings, while retaining familiar physical buttons.

That mix became especially tangible in Tearaway, whose papercraft world responded to the handheld's distinctive inputs. Other games used the screen for larger familiar adventures or smaller independent experiences. The Vita is worth examining as a designed object: a device that placed conventional controls and unusual surfaces together, then left developers to decide which combinations mattered.

entries.title: Wii U
entries.subtitle: Two screens, different points of view
entries.summary: A screen inside the controller gave the player holding it information that the rest of the room could not see.
body: Wii U's most conspicuous object was its GamePad: a controller built around a touchscreen. The idea introduced a practical problem as well as a new canvas. The console had to send pictures and sound wirelessly while responding quickly enough for a button press to feel immediate. The GamePad displayed images produced by the console; it was not a separate handheld running the same game on its own.

That second view could change the relationships between players. In Nintendo Land, the person holding the GamePad could have different information or a different role from people watching the television. Designers were not simply duplicating the picture on a smaller screen. They were deciding what each player should be allowed to know, then using that difference for cooperation or competition.

Nintendo also reworked the controller's shape and grips as it balanced comfort, weight and the appearance of an object intended for the living room. Wii U launched in North America on 18 November 2012, followed by Europe on 30 November and Japan on 8 December. Its history joins an unusual physical design to a clear creative question: what becomes possible when people share a game without sharing every view of it?

entries.title: Nintendo Entertainment System

release_dates.region: North American initial release; rollout continued subsequently
European rollout began; dates varied by country

entries.subtitle: A familiar world in a different box
entries.summary: The grey NES carried Nintendo's cartridge library into new living rooms, with a different identity from Japan's Famicom.
body: Nintendo brought the Nintendo Entertainment System to North America in 1985. It followed the Japanese Family Computer, or Famicom, introduced in 1983, but presented that platform in a different physical form. The grey front-loading case, detachable controllers and long cartridges belong to the western NES story. They should not be mistaken for the red-and-white machine's earlier Japanese debut.

Its small controller concentrated play around a directional pad and two main action buttons. Across the growing library, those few inputs could mean running and jumping, exploring a maze or choosing when to fight. Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda and Metroid helped give Nintendo's characters and worlds a place in everyday home life.

The European rollout began in 1986, with national markets following different schedules. The machine's history is therefore more than one release date or one claim to have transformed a market. It is also the story of how the same games reached different households through different objects, packaging and local experiences.

entries.title: Super Nintendo — PAL edition

release_dates.region: European/PAL rollout; no single country-specific day asserted

entries.subtitle: More colour, more room to play
entries.summary: Nintendo's 16-bit generation reached European homes with a rounded case, colourful buttons and a library that stretched across very different kinds of worlds.
body: For European players, the Super Nintendo arrived in 1992. The PAL machine kept the rounded outline and multicolour controller buttons associated with the Japanese Super Famicom, rather than the angular purple-button design sold in North America. This exhibit follows that regional object, not an invented worldwide launch shared by every version.

The controller expanded the familiar directional pad and face buttons with shoulder buttons under the player's index fingers. Stereo sound and richer imagery gave designers more room, but the results were not confined to spectacle. Super Mario World offered a colourful landscape of secrets; A Link to the Past built an adventure around revisiting places with new abilities; Super Metroid made exploration feel lonely and uncertain.

F-Zero and Super Mario Kart turned the new machine towards a different sensation: speed and competition. Looking across this library, the generational change becomes visible through contrasts. A single cartridge system could hold races, long journeys and quiet discoveries, each asking something different of the same controller.

entries.title: Sega Saturn

release_dates.region: North America; month precision in cited Sega retrospective

entries.subtitle: The arcade has more than one future
entries.summary: Saturn brought Sega's arcade ambitions home while giving richly drawn 2 D games a place beside the new polygon worlds.
body: Sega Saturn launched in Japan on 22 November 1994 with Virtua Fighter among its defining attractions. Sega's arcade fighting game had made three-dimensional characters a compelling new spectacle. Bringing that kind of experience into the home became one of the machine's central promises.

Yet Saturn's identity cannot be reduced to the arrival of polygons. Its library also became a home for 2 D fighting games and shooters, supported in some cases by additional memory cartridges. Sega's own retrospective places those games alongside arcade adaptations such as Daytona USA, Sega Rally Championship and Virtua Fighter 2. The new generation could develop several visual languages at once.

The platform reached North America in 1995, in a market where Sega was also trying to extend the life of Genesis through the 32 X. Those overlapping plans made the transition complicated. The grey Japanese launch machine and black western versions also remind us that Saturn was never encountered in exactly the same way everywhere: its hardware, software library and position in the market depended on where a player lived.

entries.title: Xbox One

release_dates.region: Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Mexico, New Zealand, Spain, UK and USA

entries.subtitle: A console at the centre of the room
entries.summary: Microsoft presented Xbox One as a shared home-entertainment hub, placing games beside television, communication and the Kinect sensor.
body: Xbox One arrived on 22 November 2013 in 13 initial markets. Microsoft presented it as a machine for more than games: television, streaming, Skype and voice control were part of the same living-room proposal. The original large black console and Kinect sensor gave that ambition a physical form.

The games still had to establish what this new Xbox felt like to play. Forza Motorsport 5 focused on cars and circuits, Dead Rising 3 filled its setting with zombies, and Ryse: Son of Rome pursued a cinematic historical spectacle. Around them, features such as Game DVR and Upload made recording and circulating play part of the platform's everyday activity.

The original model displayed here belongs to that 2013 beginning, before the smaller Xbox One S and the later One X. Its story captures a particular moment when a console maker tried to gather many activities beneath one interface. The object makes those priorities readable: a games machine designed to claim a broad place beneath the television.

entries.title: Xbox Series X

release_dates.region: Initial international launch markets; availability varied by territory

entries.subtitle: A new generation carries its library forward
entries.summary: Fast storage, a tower-shaped case and compatibility with older games made continuity part of Microsoft's next-generation argument.
body: Xbox Series X launched on 10 November 2020 alongside the smaller Series S. Microsoft described the generation through power, speed and compatibility. The new console was intended to deliver more detailed games, but also to reduce waiting and bring existing collections into the new hardware generation.

Its solid-state storage supported faster loading and Quick Resume, which could keep several supported games ready to continue. A disc drive remained part of the original Series X design. For players with compatible physical games, the old collection could still have a place beside digital purchases and subscription libraries.

The tall black body gave those ambitions a different silhouette from the broad original Xbox One. Yet the platform's argument was partly about avoiding a complete break: compatible games, accessories and saved progress could travel forward. This exhibit follows that combination of change and continuity, rather than treating a console generation as nothing more than a reset of technical specifications.

entries.title: Xbox Series S

release_dates.region: Initial international launch markets; availability varied by territory

entries.subtitle: A smaller doorway into the same generation
entries.summary: The compact, disc-free Series S traded a higher rendering target for a lower launch price while sharing the generation's core storage and processing approach.
body: Xbox Series S launched on 10 November 2020 as a second route into the same generation as Series X. Its small white case and large black circular vent made the difference visible. At a US launch price of$299, it was positioned below the$499 Series X, with a lower rendering target rather than a separate catalogue of next-generation games.

The console retained the generation's emphasis on fast storage and Quick Resume. Microsoft designed Series S around similar CPU capability and the same input/output performance as Series X, allowing developers to scale imagery while keeping those shared foundations. That distinction mattered more than a simple comparison of how many pixels appeared on screen.

There was no disc drive. A player's library therefore depended on digital purchases, compatible digital games and services, rather than inserting an existing disc. The original 2020 Series S is a useful museum object because it makes an economic and cultural choice tangible: a smaller, less expensive console whose access to games is entirely digital.

entries.title: Nintendo DSi
entries.subtitle: A handheld becomes a personal collection
entries.summary: Cameras, sound tools and downloadable software gave the DS family another way to make a handheld feel like your own.
body: The original Nintendo DS had introduced its two-screen format in North America in November 2004. DSi was a later revision, first released in Japan on 1 November 2008. Europe followed on 3 April 2009 and North America two days later. Its name belongs to that particular machine, rather than to the beginning of the entire DS family.

Nintendo put two cameras, sound manipulation tools and internal storage into a thinner case. A player could photograph a friend, distort the result or experiment with the pitch of a recording. These activities made the machine a small creative tool as well as a place to play cartridges. The touchscreen already familiar to DS owners now helped arrange material they had made themselves.

DSiWare added downloadable games and applications through the DSi Shop. Software could remain inside the handheld alongside personal photographs and recordings. The physical object still opened into two screens, but the collection it carried was becoming less dependent on which cartridge was in its slot. This exhibit shows the DSi revision; it should not be mistaken for the original 2004 DS or the 2006 DS Lite.

entries.title: Game Boy Advance
entries.subtitle: More room for a familiar world
entries.summary: A wider colour screen and shoulder buttons changed the shape of Game Boy, while older cartridges kept a route into its past.
body: Game Boy Advance moved the screen between the player's hands. The original horizontal model launched in Japan on 21 March 2001. Its wider colour display and new shoulder buttons made the change immediately visible, before a game had even started. Nintendo was giving developers a different canvas while keeping the familiar idea of a small machine built around interchangeable cartridges.

The transition also carried a player's collection forward. Alongside software made for its 32-bit hardware, the Advance could play earlier Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges, with compatibility qualifications noted in Nintendo's documentation. The machine connected two moments in portable play: a new display and controls, and games already kept in drawers or passed between friends.

A link cable could connect up to four systems in supported games. Some titles even allowed several people to join using one cartridge. The result depended on a physical arrangement of handhelds, cables and players rather than an invisible network. This entry concerns the original 2001 body. The folding Advance SP was a later redesign, not an alternative shape sold at the first Japanese launch.

entries.title: Nintendo 3DS
entries.subtitle: Depth without a pair of glasses
entries.summary: The familiar two-screen handheld gained a stereoscopic upper display, a Circle Pad and a new relationship with movement and space.
body: Nintendo 3DS retained a recognisable arrangement: two screens, physical buttons and a touchscreen below. Its upper display changed what that familiar object could show. Stereoscopic depth was visible without wearing special glasses, and a slider let players adjust the effect. The first Japanese systems arrived on 26 February 2011.

A Circle Pad added analogue movement beside the D-pad. Cameras, motion sensing and a gyroscope gave software further ways to respond to the world around the screen. Older DS and DSi game cards remained usable, so the new machine carried an existing library into a different set of possibilities. Not every game had to use every feature; choosing which inputs mattered remained a design decision.

The hardware's identity also appeared through later colours and special editions. Nintendo's black-and-gold Zelda 25 th Anniversary bundle reached Europe on 25 November 2011, with a Hyrule emblem and Ocarina of Time 3D. That edition belongs to the same first-year 3DS body, but its November release should not replace the February date of the original system. The larger XL and later New Nintendo 3DS designs are separate revisions.

entries.title: Nintendo 64
entries.subtitle: Learning to move through space
entries.summary: An unusual controller and four built-in ports connected the new problem of moving through 3D worlds with the familiar pleasure of playing together.
body: Nintendo 64 reached Japan on 23 June 1996. Project Reality, the development partnership announced in 1993, had become an object that players could finally put beside a television. Super Mario 64 helped explain what the change meant: an environment to explore, rather than a picture to move across. The console's launch and its earlier announcement belong at different points on this timeline.

Its controller made that transition physical. Three grips offered different ways to hold it, with an analogue stick in the centre and a trigger underneath. Moving the stick was a different action from choosing a direction on a pad. Designers could connect the direction and extent of a movement to what happened in a three-dimensional world, while familiar buttons remained within reach.

Four controller ports made another ambition visible on the front of the machine. Mario Kart 64 and Mario Party could turn the same room into a shared playing space, with friends looking at one television. Europe's release followed in March 1997. The dark original-style body displayed here represents the platform; later transparent colours and special editions gave the same underlying machine different visual identities.

entries.title: Mega Drive / Genesis
entries.subtitle: One machine, more than one identity
entries.summary: Sega's 16-bit console changed its name across regions, carrying a growing library from its Japanese launch into different markets and memories.
body: The words on the case changed as Sega's console travelled. Mega Drive launched in Japan on 29 October 1988. North America received it as Genesis the following year, while the European Mega Drive arrived in 1990. Those names describe related regional histories, rather than rival machines or one simultaneous worldwide release. The model here carries the Mega Drive wordmark.

Sega presented 16-bit hardware through the promise of stronger pictures, speed and sound. Its history also involved software makers beyond Sega itself and an expanding range of peripherals. The console was a platform around which games, accessories and different physical versions accumulated. A cartridge slot and a pair of controller ports were only part of that wider system.

Sonic the Hedgehog gave it a particularly recognisable face in 1991. Sega's own retrospective links the game's arrival to the platform's growing international popularity. Later additions such as Mega-CD explored different storage and software possibilities, while redesigned cases changed the object on the shelf. The original form factor is useful precisely because it sits near the beginning of this branching story: before a long-lived family of names and versions became a single nostalgic image.

entries.title: Xbox 360
entries.subtitle: A profile that follows you between games
entries.summary: Xbox Live, Achievements and a dashboard full of downloadable games made the console's identity extend beyond the disc currently in its drive.
body: Xbox 360 launched in North America on 22 November 2005, followed by Europe on 2 December and Japan on 10 December. Microsoft was introducing a new console, but it was also extending the role of Xbox Live. A gamer profile, messages and friends could connect experiences that otherwise belonged to separate games. The dashboard became a place to return to, rather than just a route to a disc.

Achievements gave that shared identity another visible form. Progress could contribute to a Gamerscore that travelled across games. Xbox Live Marketplace offered demonstrations, trailers and downloadable content, while Xbox Live Arcade placed smaller games directly inside the console's interface. Geometry Wars Retro Evolved and Bejeweled 2 appeared alongside other launch downloads. A game did not need a large physical box to be encountered from the sofa.

The curved original case became the object associated with this connected routine, but its colours and hardware configurations changed over time. The rotating model is a black version of that early form factor, rather than the white machine most closely associated with the 2005 launch. Keeping those details separate lets one exhibit explain both a platform's beginning and the later object an artist chose to reconstruct.

entries.title: Nintendo GameCube
entries.subtitle: A small box with room for four
entries.summary: A compact console, small optical discs and a distinctive controller gave Nintendo's next generation a recognisable physical character.
body: The indigo GameCube reached Japan on 14 September 2001. Its name described an unusually direct piece of industrial design: a compact body, a lid on top and a handle at the back. North America followed that November; Europe arrived in May 2002. A familiar object in one region could still be a new arrival somewhere else.

Inside the lid was an eight-centimetre optical disc. Across the front were four controller ports, keeping shared play visible in the hardware itself. The controller gave its buttons different shapes and sizes around a large green A button. Rather than presenting every action as an identical mark, it made the arrangement something a thumb could learn by touch.

The object also grew connections beyond its own discs. A cable linked compatible games to Game Boy Advance, while the later Game Boy Player fitted underneath and brought Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridges to a television. These accessories offered different ways to connect a portable library with the living room. The model shown here represents the original indigo case and its controller, rather than the later Panasonic Q or a special edition.

entries.title: Game Boy Color
entries.subtitle: A new screen, an old library
entries.summary: Colour changed the picture without asking players to leave their existing Game Boy cartridges behind.
body: By 1998, a Game Boy could already carry years of someone's playing life. Nintendo's next handheld had to offer a visible change without making that collection feel disposable. Game Boy Color launched in Japan on 21 October, combining a colour screen with support for original Game Boy cartridges. Continuity was part of the attraction, not simply a technical footnote.

Its appearance made the new direction easy to recognise. The case came in bright colours, including green, yellow and clear purple. The screen still relied on available light rather than a backlight, and two AA batteries powered the machine. The new experience remained attached to familiar habits: choosing a cartridge, finding a comfortable place to see the screen and carrying a small collection along.

The library crossed the boundary in more than one way. Some cartridges worked on older Game Boys as well as the Color, while others required the new machine's capabilities. An existing game and a newly designed colour game could therefore sit beside each other in the same player's bag. The green model displayed here is an artist's reconstruction of that original form, with a game image on its screen; the screen image is not a claim that every cartridge was exclusive to Game Boy Color.

entries.title: Intellivision

date.region: United States: national introduction; test market in 1979

entries.subtitle: Putting a team on the television
entries.summary: Mattel used sports, detailed animation and a different kind of controller to argue that its console could offer something beyond another game of Pong.
body: Before its national American introduction in 1980, Intellivision was tested in and around Fresno, California, during 1979. That distinction matters: the first local sale and the wider arrival were different events. The brown and woodgrain console belonged to Mattel's attempt to give the home television a more ambitious role in play.

Its controllers asked players to learn a different vocabulary. A disc registered sixteen directions, while a twelve-key pad and side buttons offered more inputs than a simple paddle. Sports helped make the argument for the hardware. Mattel's advertising compared its baseball with Atari's, while programmers worked around a less visible problem: the display hardware could draw only eight moving objects at once.

The solution depended on decisions about what needed to move and what could temporarily become part of the background. A busy playing field was an effect constructed within limits, not an unlimited canvas. The Blue Sky Rangers' retrospective describes these techniques and the people behind them. Looking at the original console alongside that account brings the commercial promise and the programming work into the same frame: a machine sold through the picture, and games made through careful compromises.

entries.title: Atari Lynx

date.region: United States: original model; limited initial availability

entries.subtitle: Turn the screen around
entries.summary: A colour handheld could change its orientation to suit the player's hands and link with other machines for shared games.
body: The first Lynx arrived in 1989, bringing a colour screen into a handheld whose broad body was very different from a Game Boy. The comparison is useful, but the Lynx deserves a closer look than a contest between two specification sheets. It proposed its own relationship between the player's hands, the display and the people nearby.

Atari's original manual explains a revealing feature: players could turn the machine around and flip its image, moving the directional pad from the left hand to the right. Games designed for a vertical screen could be held another way again. The arrangement treated orientation as a choice rather than a fixed assumption. Duplicated action buttons made that choice practical in the physical case.

A ComLynx cable connected compatible games across separate handhelds. Each player could hold a screen while taking part in the same session. Colour, orientation and linked play all had to fit inside an object powered by batteries or an adaptor. The wide original model displayed here predates the smaller Lynx II. Its unusual proportions preserve a particular answer to portable play, rather than a failed attempt to become the same object as its better-known competitor.

entries.title: Hanimex 7771

date.region: French-labelled example; year recorded by hands-on restoration documentation

release_dates.region: Documented model year; exact first-sale day and regional rollout not established

entries.subtitle: The television learns a new trick
entries.summary: Two paddles and a fixed set of games turned an ordinary television into a shared playing surface, long before the idea of a console library became familiar.
body: The French-labelled Hanimex 7771 belongs to a time when a television game could be an appliance with its games already inside. Its orange case, two detachable paddle controls and switches made the rules visible before the television was even on. A player adjusted a dial to meet a moving ball, sharing a screen with another person rather than choosing from shelves of cartridges.

A documented restoration dates this model to 1977 and shows the General Instrument AY-3-8500 chip inside. Much of the game's behaviour was concentrated in that circuit. The original connection sent its picture through a television's aerial input; getting it on screen involved tuning a channel. Decades later, restoring the sound and picture meant dealing with corroded batteries, ageing connections and a television standard many newer screens no longer receive.

The object also survives beyond private memories. France's national library recorded a Hanimex 7771 among the equipment received in a 2008 bequest. That modest entry is a reminder of what preservation can include: not only celebrated software, but the machines, connectors and ordinary domestic objects that made an evening's play possible. This is its own console, not a substitute model for the earlier Magnavox Odyssey.
